title: Same Person, Different Seats: Why Behaviour Follows Roles
topic: tư duy: vai trò, tình huống và lỗi quy kết cơ bản
unit: Chặng 1/12 · Ngôi nhà & gia đình Việt · Tuần 1/4: Gia đình, họ hàng & xưng hô
summary: People are less consistent across situations than we assume, yet they are consistent in 'if… then…' patterns. Drawing on Mischel and Shoda, Goffman and the quizmaster study, this piece shows how roles act as powerful situations, why we blame people for their seats (the fundamental attribution error), and how to read relatives and colleagues as patterns rather than labels.
body:
Picture an uncle at a death-anniversary meal (*đám giỗ*). At the head of the tray he is grave, slow-spoken, the one who lights the incense and decides when everyone may eat. Two hours later, on the porch with his nephews, he is cracking jokes and arguing about football. On Monday, at the district office where he is a deputy head, he is brisk and slightly impatient. At home, according to his wife, he cannot find his own socks.

Which one is the "real" uncle? The tempting answer is that one of these is genuine and the others are masks. This piece argues for a more useful answer: all four are real, and the pattern across them is the person. Learning to see that pattern is one of the most practical thinking tools for anyone who deals with families, offices and the public.

## The puzzle: people are less consistent than we think

We talk about people as if they carry fixed traits around: *he is strict*, *she is generous*, *that colleague is difficult*. Psychologists took this idea seriously and went looking for the consistency. The results were awkward.

As early as 1929, the psychologist Theodore Newcomb watched 51 boys at a summer camp across 21 situations, looking at behaviours that should all reflect the same underlying trait. The average correlation of a boy's behaviour from one situation to another was only about 0.14, which is very low. A boy who was talkative at lunch was not reliably talkative at the campfire.

In 1968, Walter Mischel pulled together decades of such findings in *Personality and Assessment*. His conclusion upset the field: for many characteristics, such as moral behaviour, attitudes and aggression, behaviour in one situation predicted behaviour in another only weakly. Intelligence was fairly stable; much else was not. This became known as the "personality paradox": we feel strongly that people have consistent characters, but their behaviour from situation to situation varies a great deal.

## The resolution: consistency lives in "if… then…" patterns

Mischel did not conclude that personality is an illusion. Working with Yuichi Shoda, he argued that researchers had been looking for consistency in the wrong place. In a 1995 paper in *Psychological Review*, they proposed that a person's stable character shows up not as the same behaviour everywhere, but as a stable **profile** of the form: *if situation A, then I do X; but if situation B, then I do Y*. They called these profiles **behavioural signatures**.

The evidence came from another camp, a residential programme for children with problems of aggression and self-control. Instead of rating each child as simply "aggressive" or "not aggressive", researchers recorded behaviour separately across types of situation: when teased or provoked by peers, when warned by adults, when approached positively by peers, when praised. Each child turned out to have a distinctive and fairly stable shape. As Mischel later put it, the same child who is among the least aggressive when teased may be known for flaring up when flattered and praised. Another child might show the reverse. Averaged together, the two look similar. Seen as profiles, they are completely different people.

So there are two kinds of consistency. The first is the average level (how aggressive overall). The second is the shape: *where* and *with whom* the behaviour rises or falls. The second kind is often more stable and more informative.

## Roles are the strongest "situations" of all

If situations shape behaviour, social **roles** are among the most powerful situations there are. A role is a seat with a script: expectations about what the person in that seat should say, do and feel.

The sociologist Erving Goffman made this vivid in *The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life* (first published in Scotland in 1956, then in the United States in 1959). He described social life in theatrical terms. In the **front region** we perform for an audience, managing the impression we give; in the **back region** we relax, rehearse and drop parts of the role. We often perform as **teams**: the family hosting guests at Tết, the staff of an office facing citizens at the counter. Goffman's point was not that people are fake. It was that being a competent member of society *means* playing roles well.

Vietnamese family life is full of clearly scripted seats: the eldest son of the senior line (*con trưởng*, *trưởng họ*) who leads the rituals; the daughter-in-law (*con dâu*) in her husband's family, especially in the first years; the youngest son who stays home to care for his parents; the paternal aunt (*cô*) whose word carries weight in her brother's household. The forms of address we studied this week (*xưng hô*) are themselves role labels. When a 30-year-old calls a 25-year-old *anh* because of family rank (*vai vế*), the word places both of them in seats, and their behaviour tends to follow.

That is why the uncle at the start can be grave at the altar and playful on the porch. The altar is a front region with a solemn script; the porch with the nephews is a back region with a relaxed one.

## The trap: blaming the person for the seat

Here is where this becomes a thinking tool rather than just an interesting fact. Humans have a strong tendency to explain behaviour by character and to underweight the situation. The psychologist Lee Ross named this the **fundamental attribution error** in 1977.

The classic early demonstration came from the psychologists Jones and Harris in 1967. Participants read essays for or against Fidel Castro. Some were told the writer had chosen the position freely; others were told the position had been assigned by a coin toss. Even when they knew the writer had no choice, participants still judged a pro-Castro writer as more pro-Castro.

An even sharper study is about roles directly. In 1977, Ross and his colleagues Teresa Amabile and J. L. Steinmetz ran a quiz game at Stanford. Pairs of students drew cards to become either "questioner" or "contestant". The questioner wrote ten challenging questions from his or her own knowledge; the contestant tried to answer. Contestants got about four out of ten right on average. Then everyone rated general knowledge on a 100-point scale. Contestants rated questioners at about 67 and themselves well below that. Observers watching the game rated questioners at about 82 and contestants at about 49. Yet the role was assigned randomly, and on a separate quiz the two groups scored almost exactly the same (about 7.75 versus 7.71 out of 15). Everyone, including the people who knew the roles had been drawn from a deck, mistook the advantage of the seat for the quality of the person.

Daily life is full of quizmaster effects. The official behind the counter seems knowledgeable and the citizen in front seems confused, but the official knows the forms because it is his job, and he would be just as lost at a hospital billing desk. The mother-in-law seems "controlling" and the new daughter-in-law seems "timid", but both may be playing seats that the household arranged long before either woman arrived.

## Applying it: one family story, two explanations

Take a common story. In a family, the eldest son's wife does most of the cooking for every *đám giỗ*. The younger sisters-in-law arrive late and leave early. Over the years, the eldest daughter-in-law becomes known as "sharp-tongued", and the others as "spoiled".

**Person explanation**: she has a difficult temper; they are lazy.

**Seat explanation**: the eldest son's household is expected to host the rituals, so his wife holds a seat with heavy duties and little recognition. The younger couples live farther away, and the custom gives them a lighter script. Anyone placed in the eldest daughter-in-law's seat for fifteen years might become sharp-tongued. Anyone in the younger seats might drift toward arriving late.

The seat explanation does not excuse rudeness. But it changes what you would try. Instead of hoping the eldest daughter-in-law becomes "nicer", the family could change the seat: rotate the cooking, have each household bring a dish, publicly thank her in front of the elders. Structural problems need structural fixes.

The same reasoning works at the office. A colleague who is curt at the reception desk on Monday mornings may be perfectly warm at lunch. Before concluding "she is cold", check the seat: forty people waiting, a system that keeps crashing, a supervisor watching the queue.

## Three cautions

1. **Seats do not erase people.** Mischel's whole point was that individuals differ in *how* they respond to the same situation. Two people in the same role still show different signatures. The goal is to see both: the seat and the person's particular way of filling it.
2. **Be careful with famous dramatic studies.** You may have heard of the Stanford prison experiment, often cited to show that roles turn ordinary people cruel. Later investigators have raised serious doubts about how it was run, so it is a weak foundation. The quiz study and the camp research make the point more carefully.
3. **Do not use roles as your own excuse.** "I was only doing my job" is the seat explanation turned into a shield. Understanding the pressure of a role is the beginning of responsibility, not the end of it.

## How to practise

- **The swap test.** When someone's behaviour irritates you, ask: *if almost anyone were put in that seat, with those pressures and that audience, would they act roughly the same?* If yes, look at the seat first.
- **Write one "if… then…" profile.** Choose someone you find puzzling, a relative or a colleague. Write three lines: "If ___, then she ___." For example: "If her mother-in-law is present, then she goes quiet. If she is with her own sisters, then she leads the conversation. If someone praises her cooking, then she brushes it off." You will usually find that the person is more consistent than you thought, just not in the way you were measuring.
- **Notice front and back regions.** At the next family gathering, watch where people's manner changes: the altar versus the kitchen, the main tray versus the porch. Note who gets a back region and who never does. The people with no back region are often the ones under the most strain.
- **Check your own seats.** List the roles you play in a week: daughter, niece, colleague, junior, public servant at the counter, friend. Ask which one most changes how you speak. That self-knowledge makes it easier to switch seats on purpose rather than by habit.

The uncle who is grave at the altar and silly on the porch is not two people. He is one person with a signature: solemn when he holds the incense, playful when the role is put down. Once you start reading people as patterns across seats rather than fixed labels, family gatherings and office corridors both become easier to understand, and kinder.

connect.why: That piece introduced roles as part of the family system and the 'swap the person for the role' move; this one gives the research behind it and the if… then… tool.
Forms of address set by family rank are role labels; this piece explains why people's behaviour shifts with the seat those words assign.
Reading whether a relative is greeting, worrying or comparing is an exercise in seeing the seat and the situation before judging the person.

check.q: What is the 'personality paradox', and how did Mischel and Shoda resolve it?
check.a: We feel people have consistent traits, but their behaviour varies a lot across situations. Mischel and Shoda argued the consistency lies in stable if… then… profiles (behavioural signatures), not in identical behaviour everywhere.

check.q: In the 1977 quizmaster study, why did observers rate questioners as far more knowledgeable, and what does that show?
check.a: Questioners asked questions from their own knowledge, so they looked clever, though roles were drawn at random and both groups scored the same on a separate quiz. People mistook the advantage of a role for the quality of the person: the fundamental attribution error.

check.q: Apply the swap test to an eldest daughter-in-law who has become 'sharp-tongued' after years of hosting every đám giỗ.
check.a: Ask whether almost anyone in that seat, with heavy duties and little recognition, would become similar. If so, change the seat (rotate cooking, share dishes, thank her publicly) rather than only blaming her character.

try: This week, write a three-line if… then… profile for one relative or colleague who puzzles you, then watch them once in a different setting to see whether the profile holds.
